why: A language-learning software market of about $490 million split across individuals, schools and employers, with modest growth forecasts, is believable.

Sector gains of 0.2 to 0.7 percentage points of GDP growth over 10 years from apprenticeships, applied to a $450bn economy, are believable, and the 100% bars only show each sector's direct and indirect split of those points.
All four score pies sum to 100%, and 1,100 respondents making up 22% of a tool-hire depot's roughly 5,000 accounts is believable.
A fast-growing satellite crop-mapping firm with revenue rising from $28m to $134m and losses narrowing from -149% to -14% is a believable loss-making growth company.
Outdoor brands with 11 to 18 tent models making $3m to $14m in tent profits is believable.
An online wine merchant with 350,000 new customers, orders of about $64 to $76 and first-year profit of $1 to $34 per customer fits a thin-margin retailer.
Engine oil at $12 to $14 a litre to garages is high but within a factor of two of trade prices, and orders of 20 crates worth about $1,000 to $4,000 are believable.
Market shares of 0.3% to 7.7% and profit margins of 8% to 33% for a solar panel maker's foothold markets are believable.
A university-town bike workshop with about €41,000 monthly revenue from roughly 720 repairs (about €58 each) is believable, and the stated margins match revenue minus costs.
52,000 claims from 40.5k landlords (the groups add up), with about £12.5m in handling costs, works out to about £240 per claim, which is believable for a landlord insurer.
